paragraphs: Implicit neural representations encode an input as a neural network that maps coordinates to values. Classification then operates on this continuous representation. The paper investigates whether this change in representation provides protection against adversarial input perturbations, addressing a robustness question that has received relatively little systematic study.

Testing these pipelines is difficult because producing the representation requires training a separate network for each input. An attack that follows gradients through this process must contend with optimization inside the classifier’s forward computation. The authors develop surrogate models that approximate the representation-generation process, spreading its cost across inputs. They also introduce techniques that reduce the cost of training these surrogates.

Using this attack approach, the authors find that classification accuracy falls to nearly zero under adversarial perturbations in their study. Countermeasures developed for discrete representations provide limited protection. The findings challenge earlier robustness claims and show why expensive attack computation can obscure vulnerabilities: making a pipeline difficult to attack computationally does not establish that its representations resist adversarial changes.
icml-2026-adversarial-robustness-of-impl.tldr: Surrogate attacks reveal severe adversarial vulnerabilities in classifiers that encode inputs as implicit neural representations.

paragraphs: Using an externally hosted language model can expose sensitive text when prompts, outputs, or training examples cross the API boundary. AlienLM introduces a privacy layer that translates text into an alternative vocabulary before the model processes it. The translation uses a one-to-one mapping, allowing the client to recover the original text without information loss.

A reversible vocabulary mapping alone does not make a model useful on the transformed language. Alien Adaptation Training adapts the target model to work directly with these inputs through standard fine-tuning APIs. This makes the approach applicable under API-only access, without requiring the user to modify the provider’s internal model implementation.

Across four model backbones and seven benchmarks, AlienLM preserves more than 81% of plaintext-oracle performance on average and substantially exceeds the stated mapping baselines. In the evaluated attacks, adversaries equipped with model weights, corpus statistics, and learned inverse translation recover fewer than 0.22% of transformed tokens. These empirical results support reduced plaintext exposure alongside useful task performance; they do not establish a universal guarantee against recovery.
icml-2026-alienlm-alienization-of-langua.tldr: AlienLM adapts API-accessed models to reversible vocabulary-transformed text, retaining useful performance while resisting the evaluated recovery attacks.

paragraphs: Long reasoning traces make language models retain increasingly large key-value caches, creating a memory bottleneck. Compression methods often use recent attention queries to predict which earlier information will matter next. This paper finds that the assumption can fail during extended reasoning, when particular tokens revisit distant context such as an early problem-solving plan.

The authors observe that queries associated with these revisiting tokens fall into a small number of similarity groups. BeaconKV keeps compact representatives of global query groups, called beacon queries, and uses them to anticipate which cached entries may be needed again. It therefore preserves information about recurring attention patterns without retaining the complete query history or requiring additional training.

Across four open-source reasoning models and multiple benchmarks, BeaconKV generally performs better than existing cache-compression methods. The reported results include up to 5.8-fold memory reduction with accuracy close to the full-cache setting, and throughput improvements exceeding 4.3-fold. The central implication is that compression benefits from anticipating returns to earlier reasoning, rather than estimating relevance solely from the most recent steps.
icml-2026-beaconkv-key-value-cache-compr.tldr: BeaconKV compresses reasoning-model caches using representative attention queries that anticipate revisits to earlier context.

paragraphs: The same search query can express different needs for different people, and a useful answer must also match how each person prefers information to be presented. BESPOKE addresses the difficulty of evaluating these aspects of personalization in language models that use search. Its focus is whether responses fit a user’s information needs and preferences.

The benchmark draws on authentic chat and search histories supplied directly by human participants. Through sustained annotation, participants contribute their histories, write queries with detailed descriptions of what they need, and assess generated responses. Those assessments include both fine-grained preference scores and diagnostic feedback, connecting the evaluation to the people whose preferences the system is meant to understand.

This design provides more informative evidence than a single overall response score: the feedback can help characterize where an answer does or does not satisfy a user. The authors use BESPOKE for systematic analyses of personalization in information-seeking tasks. The stated contribution is an evaluation foundation and associated findings about effective personalization, rather than a new personalization model or a quantified performance improvement.
icml-2026-bespoke-benchmark-for-search-a.tldr: BESPOKE evaluates personalized search responses using authentic user histories, detailed preference scores, and human diagnostic feedback.

paragraphs: Reward-maximizing training can improve language-model reasoning while reducing the diversity of generated answers. GFlowNet approaches instead train models to match a target distribution and learn its partition function, a quantity used to normalize that distribution. This paper asks whether the learned quantity can also help decide which questions deserve training effort.

The authors establish a theoretical relationship between the partition function and estimates of each prompt’s expected reward, interpreted here as online accuracy. Their PACED-RL framework uses those estimates to prioritize informative prompts. It also prioritizes replay according to errors in the accuracy estimates, directing additional learning toward cases where those estimates need improvement.

Both mechanisms reuse information already generated during GFlowNet optimization, allowing their computational overhead to be absorbed into the existing training process. Experiments across diverse benchmarks report strong performance improvements over GRPO and earlier GFlowNet methods. The contribution is a way to make distribution-matching training more sample efficient by treating a learned normalization quantity as a useful signal about question difficulty and the progress of learning.
icml-2026-beyond-normalization-rethinkin.tldr: PACED-RL reuses a GFlowNet’s learned partition function to estimate prompt accuracy and prioritize more informative training.

paragraphs: Multi-bit text watermarks embed a recoverable message in generated text. Recovering a candidate message, however, is different from establishing that a watermark is actually present. The paper finds that existing extractors based on error-correcting codes can confuse these tasks, producing extremely high false-positive rates. Adding rejection thresholds can then reduce detection sensitivity to chance levels.

BREW separates the process into message estimation and designated verification. Independent votes from text blocks first produce a candidate payload without knowing it in advance. A second stage shifts verification windows to check that payload while accounting for local edits. This gives the method a distinct step for validating evidence of a watermark.

Under 10% synonym substitution, the reported true-positive rate is 0.965 at a false-positive rate of 0.02. This result supports the authors’ claim that unreliable detection is a fixable structural problem in the evaluated decoding-centered designs, rather than an unavoidable consequence of carrying multiple bits. The framework is model-agnostic and combines theoretical grounding with empirical evidence for more reliable watermark verification.
icml-2026-block-wise-codeword-embedding-.tldr: BREW separates watermark-message recovery from verification to improve reliable detection after local text edits.

paragraphs: Conversational query reformulation rewrites a dialogue query into a form that retrieves information more effectively. Training these systems commonly depends on reference passages that identify the desired supporting material. Those passages can be difficult to obtain in practical settings, even when conversation datasets already contain users’ questions and the responses they received.

DualReform uses those available responses to infer pseudo reference passages for preference optimization. Its second component uses a query-reformulation model to refine the responses themselves, drawing on the shared objectives of response refinement and query rewriting. Together, the two components construct training guidance from query-response data without requiring gold reference passages.

The authors report retrieval accuracy reaching 96.9–99.1% of the level attainable with reference passages, alongside gains of up to 31.6% over the stated state-of-the-art method. These findings suggest that useful retrieval-oriented supervision can be recovered from ordinary conversational records. The approach removes the requirement for gold passages while still using inferred passages as an intermediate source of training guidance.
icml-2026-breaking-the-reference-bottlen.tldr: DualReform trains conversational query rewriting with response-derived pseudo passages, approaching gold-reference retrieval performance.

paragraphs: Designing a heterogeneous catalyst requires considering both its surface and the species interacting with that surface. These components are coupled: surface geometry and adsorbate interactions jointly shape the interface. CatFlow addresses this coupling with a flow-matching model for generating new catalyst structures and predicting slab-adsorbate arrangements.

The model represents the complex through a factorization based on primitive cells. This reduces the number of variables it must learn by an average factor of 9.2 while explicitly representing the surface orientation at the interface. The representation therefore combines a smaller learning problem with information about how the catalyst surface and adsorbed species are arranged together.

On the Open Catalyst 2020 dataset, CatFlow generates structures with significantly better structural fidelity than the autoregressive and sequential baselines evaluated. Additional experiments find adsorption-energy distributions consistent with physically plausible interfaces, and generated structures closer to thermodynamic local minima. These results support the usefulness of jointly modeling the interface and its geometric organization for producing physically plausible candidate catalyst structures.
icml-2026-catflow-co-generation-of-slab-.tldr: CatFlow jointly generates catalyst surfaces and adsorbates using a compact representation that improves structural and energetic plausibility.

paragraphs: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning aims to learn goal-reaching behavior from a fixed collection of experience. Reaching unfamiliar goals in changed contexts requires recombining what that experience teaches. Existing approaches often stitch together temporally contiguous trajectory segments, which can restrict their ability to compose behavior across different contexts.

This paper formalizes analogy transduction: constructing a new plan by combining a task-related analogy with a given context. Its proposed representation captures the changes associated with optimal task execution while remaining invariant to contextual differences. Within the authors’ theoretical framework, that representation is sufficient for optimal goal reaching, providing a basis for transferring task changes across contexts.

The method also addresses the practical difficulty of combining analogies and contexts that were never observed together. Experiments in OGBench manipulation environments show substantial gains over prior methods that do not perform analogy transduction. The results support learning transferable descriptions of task change as a route to composing new behavior from limited offline data, beyond the combinations directly represented in training experience.
icml-2026-compositional-transduction-wit.tldr: The method combines context-invariant task analogies with new contexts to improve offline goal-reaching generalization.

paragraphs: Vision-language-action models adapt rich visual and language representations for robot control. Those representations may nevertheless be insufficiently sensitive to signals that matter for manipulation, including actions and the robot’s own physical state. This paper introduces an additional training objective intended to make the learned representations more responsive to those control-relevant distinctions.

Robot State-aware Contrastive Loss uses relative distances between proprioceptive states as soft supervision. In effect, relationships among the robot’s states provide guidance about how its internal representations should relate to one another. The loss supplements the original action-prediction objective and is designed as a lightweight addition compatible with standard vision-language-action training pipelines.

The authors report substantial improvements for the evaluated models, reaching 69.7% on RoboCasa-Kitchen and increasing success on challenging real-robot manipulation tasks from 45.0% to 58.3%. These findings suggest that explicitly organizing representations around robot-state information can improve control. The contribution is a relatively simple training regularizer that helps connect pretrained visual-language features to the physical distinctions required for successful action.
icml-2026-contrastive-representation-reg.tldr: A robot-state-aware contrastive loss improves vision-language-action representations and manipulation success.

paragraphs: Long conversation histories can make a language model’s key-value cache exceed device memory. Compressing the cache only after processing the entire history does not control the peak memory needed to get there. Separately, retaining information according to one query can discard material that becomes relevant in later conversational turns.

EpiCache addresses both problems without additional model training. It processes the history in blocks to bound cache growth during prefill. It also groups the conversation into coherent episodes and evicts cached entries separately within those episodes. This organization is designed to preserve topic-relevant context under a fixed memory budget while avoiding a cache shaped entirely around a single question.

Across LongMemEval, Realtalk, and LoCoMo, the authors report accuracy improvements of up to 30% and near-full-cache accuracy with four- to six-fold compression. Reported latency and peak-memory reductions reach factors of 2.4 and 3.7, respectively. The findings show the value of managing memory throughout context processing and retaining the episodic structure of conversations when supporting long-term question answering.
icml-2026-epicache-episodic-kv-cache-man.tldr: EpiCache combines block-wise processing with episode-specific cache compression to support long conversations under fixed memory budgets.

paragraphs: A generative model that can identify weak parts of its own output has an opportunity to revise them during inference. Masked diffusion models are promising for this kind of correction, but their ability to assess individual token quality is not well understood. Previous approaches have required substantial model changes or relied on imprecise quality indicators.

PRISM adds a lightweight remasking mechanism to pretrained masked diffusion models. The authors define a self-correction loss and prove that it learns per-token quality scores. Those scores are computed in the same forward pass as the diffusion model and identify low-quality tokens for correction. The approach does not require reinforcement learning or a separate verifier.

The empirical evaluation spans Sudoku, unconditional text generation with a 170-million-parameter model, and code generation with the 8-billion-parameter LLaDA model. The authors report improved inference across these domains and scales. The theoretical result concerns learning token-quality scores; the empirical results demonstrate the practical value of using those scores to guide revision across several types of discrete generation.
icml-2026-fine-tuning-masked-diffusion-f.tldr: PRISM learns token-quality scores that guide inference-time remasking and self-correction in pretrained masked diffusion models.

paragraphs: In a decoupled bandit problem, a learner makes two choices each round: an option to explore and an option to exploit. It observes the loss of the explored option without paying that loss, while paying the exploited option’s loss without observing it. Separating information gathering from action creates a distinctive learning problem.

The paper proposes an efficient Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader policy with guarantees in both stochastic and adversarial regimes. It achieves constant regret in the stochastic setting and optimal regret of order square root of KT in the adversarial setting, where K is the number of arms and T the number of rounds. These guarantees concern performance relative to the comparison action captured by regret.

The policy avoids convex optimization used by earlier methods with both types of guarantee, as well as resampling procedures common in perturbed-leader bandit algorithms. Experiments confirm substantial computational savings and better regret performance in both evaluated regimes. The contribution combines strong theoretical behavior with an implementation approach that preserves the computational appeal of perturbed-leader methods.
icml-2026-follow-the-perturbed-leader-fo.tldr: An efficient perturbed-leader policy achieves strong stochastic and adversarial regret guarantees for decoupled bandits without optimization or resampling overhead.

paragraphs: If a language model behaves like a coherent Bayesian predictor, its changing predictive beliefs should satisfy a condition called the martingale property. Roughly, its expected future belief should agree with its current belief. This paper examines that condition in ordinary multiple-choice question answering, where the discrete answer space allows exact predictive distributions to be computed.

The authors introduce prompted predictive resampling, which has the model generate a sequence of answers to the same question. They observe systematic belief drift early in this process, indicating violations of the coherence condition. Empirically, sufficient additional resampling leads the process to stabilize and converge to a coherent predictive distribution.

Building on this observation, the paper proposes seed-answer prompting to accelerate stabilization and a fine-tuning loss that incorporates self-consistency into the model. Across multiple-choice benchmarks, these methods substantially reduce drift and improve predictive coherence without sacrificing accuracy. The findings concern the consistency of the model’s evolving answer probabilities, providing a way to study and improve behavior beyond whether a final answer is correct.
icml-2026-from-drift-to-coherence-stabil.tldr: Repeated answer resampling reveals early belief drift, motivating prompting and fine-tuning methods that improve predictive coherence without reducing accuracy.

paragraphs: Multi-pathway deep linear networks provide a setting for studying how different computational routes divide learned features. Analyses based on gradient flow predict that symmetry breaks and a feature becomes concentrated in one pathway. This paper shows that discrete gradient descent with a large step size can produce a different long-term outcome.

The authors prove that solutions concentrating a signal in one pathway are sharp minima. Distributing the signal across pathways reduces sharpness, with a reduction factor that decreases as pathway count and depth increase. This establishes a connection between how the network distributes information and the local geometry of its training objective.

Early training still exhibits the depth-driven specialization predicted by gradient flow. Later, oscillations at the edge of stability override that tendency and trigger a rebalancing phase, redistributing signals among pathways. The result explains why large-step gradient descent favors shared representations in the studied deep linear networks. It also shows that the continuous-time view can miss a training phase driven by discrete optimization dynamics.
icml-2026-gradient-descent-with-large-st.tldr: Large-step gradient descent can reverse early pathway specialization in deep linear networks by driving signals toward less-sharp shared solutions.

paragraphs: Understanding why a model performs differently on training and unseen data is central to improving generalization. This paper introduces local inconsistency, a measure derived from the information geometry of neural-network parameter space. Its practical attraction is that it can be computed without explicit labels, making unlabeled examples useful for assessing this aspect of model behavior.

The authors connect local inconsistency theoretically to the Fisher information matrix and the loss Hessian, linking it to established descriptions of model sensitivity and loss curvature. They also find an empirical correlation between the measure and the generalization gap. That correlation motivates incorporating local inconsistency directly into the training objective through Inconsistency-Aware Minimization, or IAM.

In standard supervised settings, IAM improves generalization and performs comparably to methods such as Sharpness-Aware Minimization. It also proves useful in semi-supervised and self-supervised settings where the inconsistency term is computed from unlabeled data. The contribution combines a label-free diagnostic with a training objective, showing how information from unlabeled examples can support generalization-oriented optimization.
icml-2026-inconsistency-aware-minimizati.tldr: IAM uses a label-free measure of local inconsistency as a training regularizer to improve generalization.

paragraphs: An observation may be distorted by an unknown transformation even when its underlying content belongs to a familiar data distribution. This paper studies how to recover an inverse transformation on general Lie groups, mathematical spaces that describe continuous transformation families. The objective is to bring the observation back into the original distribution.

Transformation-Inverting Energy Diffusion, or TIED, treats the unknown transformation probabilistically. An energy function on the data defines a Boltzmann posterior over candidate transformations. The method samples from that posterior using diffusion that stays on the transformation manifold while requiring calculations only in its associated Lie algebra. A new target-score identity makes this score-based sampling efficient.

The main application is improving pretrained networks’ robustness to transformed inputs at test time. Experiments involving image homographies and symmetries of partial differential equations show that TIED can restore transformed observations to the training distribution and outperform strong canonicalization and sampling baselines. The contribution is a geometrically consistent way to search for corrective transformations while representing uncertainty over which correction to apply.
icml-2026-inverting-data-transformations.tldr: TIED samples corrective transformations on Lie groups to restore transformed inputs and improve pretrained-model robustness at test time.

paragraphs: Detecting that a generated image contains memorized training content does not reveal which parts of the image are affected. This paper studies localization, seeking a spatially detailed account of memorization in diffusion models. Its geometric characterization links local memorization to a collapse in variation along individual coordinates.

Reduced variation alone is ambiguous because genuine constraints in the data can produce a similar pattern. To distinguish overfitting from those constraints, the authors subtract the curvature of an underfitted baseline from the curvature being examined. The baseline can be an unconditional model or a less-trained version of the same model. This comparison is intended to isolate the component associated with overfitting.

The paper also derives a score-difference proxy that gives a geometric interpretation to an existing memorization-detection metric. Experiments with Stable Diffusion compare localization against ground-truth memorization masks and outperform a prior attention-based method. The results support using differences in local geometry to identify where memorization occurs, while explicitly accounting for the ambiguity between learned data constraints and overfitting.
icml-2026-localizing-memorized-regions-i.tldr: Curvature differences against an underfitted baseline help localize memorized image regions while accounting for intrinsic data constraints.

paragraphs: Machine-learning Hamiltonian models approximate electronic structure and allow energies and forces to be computed from their predictions. Yet evaluating how closely they reconstruct a Hamiltonian does not directly establish their usefulness for those physical quantities. This paper introduces a benchmark that evaluates energies and forces obtained from predicted Hamiltonians themselves.

Within that framework, the authors propose QHFlow2, using an SO(2)-equivariant backbone and a two-stage edge update. It reduces Hamiltonian error by 40% relative to the previous best model while using fewer parameters. The architecture is assessed both on its intermediate electronic-structure prediction and on the resulting energy and force calculations.

On MD17/rMD17, QHFlow2 reaches NequIP-level force accuracy and achieves up to 20-fold lower energy mean absolute error. On QH9, its energy error is up to 20-fold lower than MACE’s. The authors also observe consistent scaling with model capacity and data, with improvements in Hamiltonian accuracy translating into better energy and force estimates. These findings support evaluating learned Hamiltonians as practical physical predictors, beyond reconstruction quality alone.
icml-2026-machine-learning-hamiltonians-.tldr: QHFlow2 improves Hamiltonian prediction and demonstrates that those gains translate into highly accurate direct energy and force calculations.

paragraphs: People often give web agents requests that leave important preferences unstated. A useful personalized agent must connect such a request to the user’s broader context. Persona2Web introduces a benchmark on the real open web for evaluating whether agents can resolve ambiguity using user history and infer preferences that are not explicitly repeated in the current request.

The benchmark combines histories that reveal preferences implicitly over long periods with ambiguous queries that depend on those preferences. Its reasoning-aware evaluation framework supports fine-grained assessment of personalization. The clarify-to-personalize principle concerns resolving uncertainty through historical context, making the connection between past behavior and present intent central to the task.

The authors test different agent architectures, underlying language models, ways of accessing history, and levels of query ambiguity. These experiments reveal challenges in personalized web-agent behavior. The contribution is a structured way to examine how agents use contextual evidence when acting on the open web, with public code and data supporting reproducibility, rather than a new agent accompanied by a claimed numerical improvement.
icml-2026-persona2web-benchmarking-perso.tldr: Persona2Web evaluates whether web agents can infer unstated user preferences from long-term history to resolve ambiguous requests.

paragraphs: Many learning pipelines have abundant pretrained representations but few labels for the actual prediction task. Those representations can be noisy proxies for the covariates the task needs. This paper studies semi-supervised regression in that setting, asking how unlabeled proxy observations can help learn a predictor when reliable labels are scarce.

The proposed estimator has two stages. It first learns kernel eigenfeatures from all available proxy covariates, including unlabeled observations. It then fits a ridge predictor using the labeled examples. Finite-sample bounds show that fast rates in the number of labeled samples can be recovered when proxy perturbations are controlled and sufficiently many unlabeled proxy observations are available.

The authors also establish distribution regression as a direct special case, with analogous guarantees when each finite bag contains enough observations. Experiments report consistent gains over supervised and semi-supervised baselines, particularly with few labels. The findings connect practical use of abundant imperfect representations to explicit conditions under which unlabeled data can support efficient learning from a small labeled set.
icml-2026-semi-supervised-learning-with-.tldr: A two-stage regression estimator uses abundant noisy proxy features to improve learning with few labels, with guarantees under controlled noise and sufficient unlabeled data.

paragraphs: Diffusion multimodal language models can fill token positions in flexible orders and revisit their outputs through iterative refinement. This gives them a different opportunity for controlling reasoning than sequential generation provides. ST-Veto uses the availability of information about all token positions at each diffusion step to improve which candidates are selected.

The method checks two kinds of evidence. A second-order Taylor prediction estimates how token confidence is evolving, allowing temporally unstable candidates to be vetoed. Image-attention mass provides a signal of visual grounding, filtering candidates with weak image support. The method then swaps rejected tokens for safer candidates instead of relying only on confidence at the current step.

Across multiple diffusion multimodal models and reasoning benchmarks, ST-Veto consistently outperforms standard decoding policies and the prior vision-language reasoning methods evaluated. Accuracy improvements reach up to 9%, with no additional training or generation cost reported. Analyses associate the gains with generation paths that have higher confidence and stronger visual grounding, supporting the value of combining temporal stability with evidence from the image.
icml-2026-st-veto-spatio-temporal-token-.tldr: ST-Veto improves multimodal diffusion reasoning by rejecting tokens with unstable confidence or weak visual grounding.

paragraphs: A generated molecule is useful for experimental drug discovery only if it can be synthesized in practice. Some GFlowNet methods enforce this requirement through predefined reaction templates and building blocks that restrict the available generation steps. The paper identifies flexibility and scalability limitations in that approach and proposes softer guidance for molecular generation.

S3-GFN generates molecules as SMILES sequences and draws on chemical priors learned from large collections of those sequences. A soft regularization signal steers generation toward regions containing both high-reward and synthesizable molecules. Training reuses samples through off-policy replay, with separate buffers of synthesizable and unsynthesizable examples supplying a contrastive learning signal.

Across diverse tasks, the authors report that at least 95% of generated molecules are synthesizable, alongside higher rewards. This provides empirical support for learning a strong preference for practical molecules without encoding all permitted chemistry as hard generation rules. The result is a high observed synthesizability rate in the experiments, while the method’s soft constraints leave generation more flexible than a predefined reaction-based action space.
icml-2026-synthesizable-molecular-genera.tldr: S3-GFN uses chemical priors and contrastive soft regularization to generate high-reward molecules with at least 95% synthesizability in the experiments.

paragraphs: This paper examines which vision-model design choices improve resistance to additive Gaussian noise. Evaluating 1,174 pretrained models, the authors identify four recurring factors: larger initial convolution kernels, resolution-dependent downsampling under a protocol that adds sensor noise before resizing, average pooling, and supervised vision transformers compared with CLIP vision transformers.

The theoretical analysis explains several of these trends. Low-pass initial kernels attenuate noise, with noise gain decreasing quadratically with kernel size. Anti-aliased downsampling reduces noise energy roughly according to the square of its factor. Average pooling is unbiased and suppresses noise with pooling area, whereas max pooling introduces a positive bias and has greater error and worst-case sensitivity in the analysis.

The authors also connect CLIP preprocessing to increased sensitivity: smaller normalization standard deviations amplify a pixel-space worst-case bound by up to 1.91 times relative to the compared preprocessing. Reported empirical gains reach 506 ranking positions and 21.6 percentage points of accuracy. The findings yield concrete guidance for Gaussian-noise robustness while preserving the relevance of the specific noise and resizing protocol.
icml-2026-unlocking-noise-resistant-visi.tldr: A large empirical study and theoretical analysis identify architecture and preprocessing choices that improve vision-model robustness to Gaussian noise.

paragraphs: Early exit can accelerate language-model generation by stopping a token’s computation before it passes through every transformer layer. But deciding when to stop can itself be expensive: evaluating the full vocabulary output head repeatedly may erase the savings. Predetermined schedules can also allocate progressively fewer layers, limiting how long generation can continue.

WAVE uses brief offline calibration to choose a layer window in which exit decisions are considered. This reduces the number of checks and avoids premature collapse to shallow layers. At the beginning of that window, a proxy output head selects a smaller vocabulary subset, reducing the work needed for subsequent exit checks. The framework requires no gradient-based training.

The proxy head reduces per-layer exit overhead by 87% relative to a full output head. Experiments on Llama-2 7B report up to 1.4-fold average speedup while preserving output quality, with compatibility with W4A16 quantization. The contribution is a practical combination of restricted checking locations and cheaper checks, showing how early exit can deliver speed gains after accounting for its own decision overhead.
icml-2026-wave-window-aware-vocabulary-e.tldr: WAVE accelerates language-model inference through calibrated exit windows and cheaper vocabulary checks without gradient-based retraining.
